Brain games try to detect skills through generalizations or abstraction. Once subscribed after compulsion, there is not much to regret - Lumosity is not a bad app. It gives a lot of interesting brain exercise. One unsolicited advice to intending subscribers: immediately after subscription, please disable the automatic renewal feature otherwise the app will continue to drain your fund. After the first year subscription, there is no way to get a refund, and at the end of the first year you will have plenty of time to envisage for a go or a halt to your subscription.

Lumosity: Brain Training is the best.

[4★] Ian Macdonald - 2021-03-13 06:09:25 (v2021.01.19.2110325, 👍14)
With 1200+ day streaks in each of Lumosity, Peak and Elevate, I'm probably better equipped than most to evaluate what are, in my view, the 3 main rivals in this field. Lumosity may be showing its age now, with its minimal UI and low resolution graphics, but after more than 3 years of daily play, the large number of games included in the package, amongst which a handful that genuinely offer a lot of replay value, provide enough appeal to keep me coming back again and again to extend my daily streak by another day. And other users must feel the same way, because my 1200+ day streak pales into insignificance next to the 2500+ boasted by some players who've been with Lumosity since the early days and clearly haven't yet lost interest. A special mention must be made here of the 'just one more go' classic, Train of Thought. In addition to the games themselves, a lot of thought has obviously gone into the other modules, which provide interesting statistics and illuminating insights into how your brain performs during the games. Your strengths and weaknesses will be highlighted, not just at the game category level (e.g. memory vs. mathematical ability), but also in the context of a single game, detailing things like near misses, etc. When I first started playing brain games, I suspected Lumosity might be the one I would end up dropping first, but it has admirably stood the test of time. The worst thing I can find to say about it is that the price of a lifetime licence is exorbitant; or was, and may even have risen since I purchased it
------------------------------------------------------------

[4★] A Google user - 2020-04-10 17:29:28 (v2020.03.27.2110315, 👍124)
Some of the games are kind of repetitive. I agree. The memory games are fairly useful, as they reflect how useful my memory is in real life. The language games to me are the most useful. I love the Contextual game, Taking Root, and Word Bubbles. When I was at the hospital with my husband in late February for a follow-up on his DBS surgery, he was required to do some more cognitive tests. I also got the opportunity to do the same but only a limited number of tests, and I was compared to people of the same age group with similar educational background. Some of these samples of tests reminded me of Lumosity; for example, Word Bubbles. I also had to remember certain images and draw them on paper. The Tidal Treasures game is very similar in terms of choosing specific images and clicking on new ones. The Train of Thought and Trouble Brewing are very good attention games that help with divided attention. I find they are challenging enough for me. The drawbacks? Familiar Faces is an excellent game for remembering names. There is nothing else like it. Unfortunately, it requires a flash player and will not work on my iPad or phone or any Mac device. I use to play it regularly on my PC, and quite enjoyed it. Another drawback is that I wish this game had the option of multi-player format. In this time of the Covid-19 crisis we are already so socially disconnected. I get tired of playing solo. One final thought: I know that only mobile Apple devices are gaming devices. It still would be nice if Lumosity were compatible with Mac laptops and desktops. Playing on an IPhone is not nearly as interesting as playing from a computer. I realize that most games are not compatible with Mac computers, but it would be great if this could change sooner rather than later.
  ↳ Lumosity (2020-04-14 21:25:25): Hi Lisa, Our games should work on a Mac laptop or desktop.  If you haven't already, we recommend reaching out to our support team at Lumosity.com/help so we can investigate this issue for you. Thanks!

For anyone who is out there looking to enhance their cognitive abilities, look no further! I am the survivor of a diffuse axonal brain injury, resulting from being hit as a pedestrian by a car. This game really comes through for me. There are many miniature games within this application. Some games focus on enhancing certain aspects of cognitive function, like multi tasking or being able to attend many different tasks simultaneously. Where as, other games focus in on the speed of accomplishing less cognitively demanding tasks. All in all, between my diet rich in good fats derived from plants to slow down any impending future cognitive decline, playing Lumosity is a daily chore that I am happy to endure. Two thumbs way up!

Ok, so.. the games that are shown in the thumbnails apparently AREN'T all in this game. You have to buy a feature called "premium" to have access to these games. I mean, I can see where they're coming from on this, since it's a "brain workout," and with most workouts, you have to pay money for them, but by installing this app, I thought I would be getting much more. Just a recommendation for the future, but I think it would be helpful to have games where you only have to watch an advertisement to unlock them. I've seen multiple games like this, and in fact, even tended to like them better when they were this way! In my opinion, this would be a great addition to your app. You don't have to listen to this comment, since there are plenty more fish in the sea, (ha, metaphorically, don't actually go scuba diving to look for fish- or maybe do if that's your thing.) I'm just trying to leave a positive vibe, and, perhaps, a recommendation that you could use later on. Thanks, and have a great day!

[4★] A Google user - 2018-05-05 20:37:05 (v2018.04.17.1910217, 👍0)
The workouts themselves are useful for the most part. My biggest criticism 
of the app is the way the stats are calculated. Many games award you 
significantly more points for completing higher levels which influences 
your score more than your actual performance (speed, accuracy, etc). Also, 
higher levels are gated by completion of lower levels. This makes tracking 
progress via the scores somewhat meaningless, as the numbers always go up. 
Only a couple games don't have this issue. Also, your LPI will increase 
just by playing more games, so it will take you a while (a few weeks?) 
without premium membership to reach your "true" LPI. I assume they do this 
on purpose to make you feel stupid so you'll buy the premium membership.

[4★] A Google user - 2018-05-04 01:19:54 (v2018.04.17.1910217, 👍1)
So far I am enjoying the app and the subscription. I do have one complaint. 
I have noticed that many of the definitions provided in the vocabulary 
related games are not as accurate as they could be. Some of the definitions 
are subject to opinion and (for me at least) are a source of confusion. An 
example would be the word part "Nat". It was defined as having to do with 
birth. Considering the words "Natural", "Nation", and "Prenatal" only one 
of those words are related to birth. The results of the confusion are 
people being trained to memorize inaccurate definitions in the attempt to 
get a higher score. The result should be a stronger ability with the 
language. Speaking of which, this is clearly an English speaking game, so 
the word siesta really is not appropriate for inclusion in the vocabulary 
related games. While being multi-lingual is certainly a worthwhile 
ambition, including Spanish words in an English game is a little 
underhanded. I don't know if Siesta is a word that has been broadly 
accepted into regular use by English speakers (like fiance). The fact that 
I am having to stop and ponder that suggests that it might not be prevalent 
enough for inclusion in an English vocabulary game. Thanks for reading my 
feedback.

Smarter brain puzzle game. Most puzzle games focus on 1-2 skills, causing monotony & stagnation. Lumosity allows your brain to work on many skills to not only challenge you and increase abilities, but by doing so creates new neuron connections which stimulates and keeps your brain young, healthy, & active. I believe it helps ward off aging diseases such as dementia. I used Lumosity in speech therapy after sustaining a TBI when a lady hit me with her truck. It was amazing to to compare baseline scores to the results just a few weeks later. My thinking skills & speed were greatly improved, & by the end of my therapy program I felt that I was sharper than before the accident. That was 2 years ago. I started feeling slow recently, so I'm back on and bought the 1 year package. My theory is correct, if you don't use your brain...you'll lose it.

In my 3rd year as a paid subscriber and I've let myself slip twice along the way. So I've gone from 0 to peak 3 times. IT REALLY WORKS and THE DIFFERENCE IS ASTRONOMICAL!  My memory and ability to think on my feet went from embarrassingly low to way above average. I no longer forget where I parked my car, put my keys and a new person's name doesn't go in one ear and out the other. I also solve problems faster and have more effective conversation with others.  Each time it took 6-8 weeks to go from zero to peak and 40-60 hours of training. I first played to my strengths and then focused on the areas I was the weakest.  For me it was a huge success. The only downside is that the changes are only long-lasting if you stick with it. Give up on it for a couple of months and you'll be right back where you started.  Overall, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND IT!

I have tried many 'brain training' apps over the years. However, this one seems to be the most consistently designed and thought up. The exercises are well packaged, the quality of the app is of a very high quality unlike some training apps which have left out a lot of good design principles. The app is very easy to use and simple. As for the exercises, they are put together really well and if you have experience with training apps you will notice the same exercises. I'm pretty sure these exercises are based off cognitive neuroscience research and although I've read they dont have thorough practical applications in real life as of yet, the games are still enjoyable to play and offer insight into your cognitive abilities.

I'm not sure why Lumosity have been in legal trouble recently and why there is bad reviews online about this great brain workout company. I have been on and off Lumosity and I'm 38. I used Lumosity consistently for one year and a half without stopping one single day when I was in college (3.4 GPA). After not playing for a whole year people still ask me how am I able to complete all my task at my current job. I monitor  8 software applications, answer phones, enter/fix issues, train people to used our software at dealerships, etc and still feel at ease after all. In two years I have moved from a cold call center agent to the corporate side of the company and still climbing. I strongly believe Lumosity has to do in part with my dedicated success. You will tell in less than a month what I'm describing if you give it a solid shot. And even if the app hasn't done anything for my mind, the games are really fun. I'm not usually interested with gaming apps, but we're seriously considering paying for a subscription.

Fun for awhile.  My Dad liked it.  When you eventually stop using it you will find it next to impossible to cancel.  They do not have an easy way out.  I'd imagine it's easier to leave a gang than cancel a Lumosity account.    There is no cancel my account button (if there is you can't find it in under an hour of searching their site and searching for help on Google.)  You have to email them to request the cancelation, and wait a couple days for someone to get back to you.    I still have not been able to cancel because I bought a family account and gave it to my Dad as a present so although I pay the annual fee, they require that my Dad cancel the account or I need to provide my payment info to verify that I actually do pay for the account.  So basically, I can log in and update my payment info so they still get paid but I can't go the other way.    I honestly believe this set up indicates a fundamental lack of confidence in their own product.    Lumosity, your product is the entire experience and the experience of leaving is absolutely miserable.

Then less than 2 weeks after the membership lapsed I received an email offering a 35% discount.   This really bothered me. It seems instead of offering a discount to their loyal members on renewal, I was only offered a discount if I did not renew. I sent a message with my concern to their support team; this was part of the reply " I am sorry if the timing of that which we sent to former members seemed insensitive or was otherwise a negative experience. As we release more product variety, we hope that users who have lapsed will give Lumosity another shot."   Over the next weeks I kept receiving discount emails, until finally I unsubscribed from all communication.   It was a disappointing end for a product that initially I found very useful and seemed to get some positive benefit.   I wonder if anyone else has the same experience.

[2★] A Google user - 2016-08-04 13:14:05 (v2.0.7103, 👍4)
Lumosity has a long way to go to making good games of skill and learning. The games start out good at the lower levels. They often turn to games of luck and speed at higher levels.   For example, "Train of Thought" produces a random stream of trains. As you get to the higher levels, the players are frequently required to change 3 or more tracks at approximately the same time. This requires lightning reflexes and speed of a professional gamer.   "Highway Hazards" is another game of luck at higher speeds. At higher speeds, the warnings appear after the car has already crashed into the hazard. The twitch reflexes of a gamer responding to the dozen pixels of a hazard as it starts to appear on the screen is useful, but even that might not be enough without a high powered system that never lags in video updates and responds to input immediately.  In the game "Organic Order", I had  found a bug. The correct answer was marked as wrong.  I provided screen shots and had to respond 3 times to their questions to make them understand the problem. Even after all that effort, I doubt any action was taken.  I would gladly give them 5 stars if they improved.

[1★] A Google user - 2015-04-03 16:03:53 (v1.1.1403, 👍14)
I loved this app until I got a new phone.  Are you kidding me?  My data is not saved for high scores and performance from the mobile app?  Think about it, you work hard to get your scores to a certain place,  (After you've paid a questionably large price tag for what amounts to be a game), only to have it all wiped out because you bought a new phone.  This is asinine.  1) there are tons of games that will cloud store your app data as part of the cost and those games are MUCH cheaper.   2) it completely exposes the thin lie that I was willing to accept, it's just a game. If you really are trying to a) monitor progress and b) build mental "strength", why would allow a data reset that essentially puts you back in kindergarten?  Not only that but it severely drops your overall scores.  How in the world does that fit into your advertised model?  I was ok with the cost.  I was ok with the illusion of brain exercises, but you seriously showed your hand on this one. Shame. Shame. Shame.

[5★] A Google user - 2015-01-27 19:57:37 (v1.0.217, 👍12)
So, it's not free, just to be clear. I wasn't looking for another ad-loaded spyware game, anyway, so that's fine by me. I didn't mind the annual subscription, because they keep adding activities and they nicely track your development. Do I believe it trains the brain? Sure, it does. The more you use any muscle, brain included, the more it "grows." The games are deceptively simple, yet challenging at the same time. You know where you stand amongst people of your age group, which —if you put vanity aside—is super useful. The program algorithm is logical and helpful and obviously built by experts, almost smart enough to be a "personal virtual trainer." I don't like all the activities (hate the raindrops), but I do them anyway, because the point is to challenge. Do I accept the studies that say these type of activities help prevent cognitive decline or help make you sharper? The smarter part might be hard to accept, but I can accept that it trains better habits. It's challenging, keeps the brain tuned, it's different from the normal activities I apply my brain to, and in that way is relaxing and useful. I hope they keep enhancing, and I give two thumbs up.

[4★] A Google user - 2014-08-15 06:20:59 (v1.0.164, 👍0)
After I survived the injured to my brain over 30 years ago, many of the skills in my cognitive domain were deeply changed. Under a speech therapist, I initially relearned how to walk, talk, read, write, & do arithmetic. But, what I didn't learn was how to describe the myriad of symptoms that were to follow, the most of which was looking 'normal' to my friends, family, strangers, and even to myself. Years passed and even as I aged toward seniority I found Lumostiy where after it took a little bit of time to work into my daily schedule, the 'games' became loads of fun. But I don't need to complete the entire suggested workout  The reason is that engaging in one of these activities is wiring the brain to successfully complete it. This neurologically plastic response to successful and quick cellular communication is recorded as performance data that I can easily access on a weekly basis, and view as a chart. This helps me build confidence in the way my cognitive skills use has changed. While I am waiting for more research to be completed about Lumostiy to prove it's impact on cognitive health, I know it is working for me. It's fun, too.   - Marlon, TBI Survivors Deserve Better
